Rita Anne Lackey, 79, of Alamogordo, New Mexico, passed away peacefully at home on November 3, 2026, surrounded by her family.

Rita was born on August 23, 1947, in Allegany, New York, to Geddes and Betty Kujaneck. She graduated from Alamogordo High School in 1965 and married Norman later that year. After she graduated from Baptist Bible College in Springfield, Missouri, the couple answered a call to serve the Lord as missionaries in Ethiopia, East Africa, where they remained until 1977. They later continued their missionary work in Puerto Rico from 1979 to 1983.

Rita was a longtime member of La Luz Bible Church, where she taught Sunday School and her church family was a cherished part of her life. She knew how much the Lord had done for her, and she loved sharing the joy of knowing Him with others.

Art was a lifelong passion for Rita. She painted and drew, and she taught art classes to many students. She also loved music and spending time outdoors.

Rita dearly loved her family. She is survived by her husband of 61 years, Norman Lackey; her children, Carissa (Pete) Pittman, Nathan Lackey, Jennifer (Alex) Burks, and Rachel (Justin) Burks; nine grandchildren; two great-grandchildren; and her brother, Dan Kujaneck.

She was preceded in death by her parents, Geddes and Betty Kujaneck; her brother, Bryan Kujaneck; and her daughter-in-law, Cynthia Lujan Lackey.

A memorial service will be held on Saturday, December 5, 2026, at 2:00 p.m. at La Luz Bible Church in La Luz, New Mexico.

item.title: Lawmakers' paycheck arrives without ethics rules; think tank maps the missing guardrails
item.description:
SANTA FE — New Mexico legislators will start drawing salaries in 2029, but the measure voters approved Nov. 3 adds no ethics rules to go with the money. A new report from Think New Mexico lays out the guardrails that are missing.

The Santa Fe think tank's new report lays out four groups of reforms: mandatory disclosure and recusal on conflicts of interest, a two-year wait before former lawmakers can lobby, broader lobbyist disclosure, and new rules on dark money and fake constituent messages.

Constitutional Amendment 4 passed roughly 62% to 38% in preliminary returns. It ties pay to the state's median household income, about $68,000, ending New Mexico's status as the last state with an unsalaried legislature. The amendment sets pay only; it contains no new rules on conflicts of interest, outside income or lobbying.

That gap is the concern Alamogordo Town News raised before the election. Its editorial board urged a no vote on Oct. 27, arguing the amendment wrote a paycheck without defining the job or the ethics standards that should come with it.

Think New Mexico's report reaches a similar conclusion: states that pay legislators generally hold them to stricter rules, and New Mexico's volunteer status has long been the excuse for loose ones.

It also points to recent scandals. On Aug. 14, former House Majority Leader Sheryl Williams Stapleton was convicted of 31 federal felonies, including bribery and money laundering, for diverting more than $2 million in education funds meant for Albuquerque students. A 2025 Garrity Group survey found only 19% of New Mexicans trust state government officials, down from 31% in 2020.

A BSP Research poll commissioned by the group, conducted July 22 to Aug. 10, found 64% of voters back paying legislators only if mandatory ethics reforms come with it.

Alamogordo Town News editor Chris Edwards laid out the case against Amendment 4 in an Oct. 27 commentary. The amendment, he wrote, sets a salary for 112 legislators without defining the work it pays for.

Nothing in the measure requires minimum hours, town halls, district offices, constituent-service standards or attendance at interim committees. It places no limit on outside income, so a member could collect the full salary while keeping a full-time career.

The commentary also put a price on the job:

About $65 an hour. Supporters cite a self-reported average of 20 hours a week. At roughly $67,800 a year, that works out to about $65 an hour.

Nearly $90,000 a year. Legislators keep their $247-a-day per diem, mileage and pension. In a 60-day session year, salary plus session per diem reaches $82,620, and passes $87,500 with 20 interim committee days.

Room for more. The amendment deletes the constitutional ban on other "perquisites or allowances," letting a future Legislature add benefits for itself.

The editorial board called for a new amendment next session that defines the job, addresses outside employment and conflicts of interest, and lets an independent citizens commission set pay.

Think New Mexico's package answers the conflict-of-interest piece of that critique. It does not address minimum duties or who sets legislative pay, which Town News flagged as equally urgent.

The centerpiece is a constitutional amendment requiring salaried legislators to recuse themselves from bills in which they have a direct financial stake, without needing their colleagues' permission.

Under current House and Senate rules, a lawmaker cannot simply recuse. The chamber must vote to excuse them. The report counts New Mexico among just nine states where recusal is discouraged, while 36 states expect it. Colorado, Oklahoma and Texas write the requirement into their constitutions.

The group wants a constitutional change rather than a statute because a February 2026 State Ethics Commission advisory opinion said each chamber controls its own members' voting, leaving a law open to challenge.

The test would be whether a bill helps or hurts a legislator more than the public at large. A teacher-legislator could vote on the overall education budget but not on a bill raising retired teachers' pensions.

The report also calls for:

Requiring legislators to disclose financial conflicts before acting on a bill, as 43 states do, following Colorado's model.

Requiring disclosure when a spouse, parent, child or sibling is paid to lobby on a bill, as the Ethics Commission has recommended, and recusal when the lobbyist is a spouse.

Rewriting the Financial Disclosure Act so officials name the specific businesses and assets behind income over $5,000, instead of broad categories like "investment income," and report honoraria and debts. Dollar amounts would stay private.

Polling found 81% support for recusal on direct conflicts and 78% for disclosing family members' lobbying.

The second proposal would bar former legislators from lobbying for pay for two years after leaving office. Today, a lawmaker could legally resign mid-session and be paid to lobby former colleagues the next day.

Thirty-seven states have such waiting periods, most of one or two years. Florida's is six. Members of Congress have been covered since 1989, and New Mexico executive branch employees have faced a one-year ban since 1993. The report would lengthen that executive branch ban to two years for consistency.

The idea has drawn bipartisan support before. A 2017 two-year ban passed the House 58-2 but died in the Senate Judiciary Committee, and Sen. Harold Pope has introduced versions in 2023, 2025 and 2026. Former Govs. Bill Richardson, a Democrat, and Susana Martinez, a Republican, both backed it.

The ban would not stop former lawmakers from advocating unpaid. Sixty-six percent of voters supported it; 10% opposed.

Registered lobbyists outnumber New Mexico legislators about six to one, and their reported spending hit a record $1.25 million by October 2025. Yet the Center for Public Integrity gave the state an F for lobbying disclosure, ranking it 43rd.

The report cites filings that reveal little. One lobbyist with 19 clients reported $22,710 spent on flowers for legislators. Another listed 31 restaurant meals for "various legislators and staff" without naming clients or bills.

Think New Mexico proposes four changes to the Lobbyist Regulation Act:

The report estimates lobbyists received more than $7.8 million in unreported pay in 2025, based on national ratios of compensation to spending.

The bill-tracking idea came close in 2025. House Bill 143, sponsored by Rep. Sarah Silva and Sen. Jeff Steinborn, passed both chambers but was vetoed by the governor. Colorado requires lobbyists to disclose a bill position within 72 hours.

State law requires groups that buy political ads to disclose their donors, but only their direct donors. The report shows how that leaves voters guessing.

New Chapter New Mexico PAC spent $438,198 in the 2026 primary; its only contributor was a nonprofit of the same name, which need not reveal its funders. Accountable New Mexico got 88.7% of its $975,500 from one nonprofit. Elevate New Mexico, which ran ads for the Project Jupiter data center, drew all of its $3.67 million from a single LLC.

The group proposes a "true source" law modeled on Arizona's Voters' Right to Know Act, approved by 72% of Arizona voters in 2022 and upheld by that state's Supreme Court in June. Big spenders would name donors over $5,000, and those donors would name their own funders until the original source is reached. Ads would list their top three donors and the share of out-of-state money. It would cover both campaign and issue ads.

The report also recommends:

Seventy-one percent of voters supported requiring ad sponsors to report their funding sources.

Most of the proposals could be passed as ordinary bills in the 60-day legislative session that opens in January. The recusal requirement would need lawmakers to put another constitutional amendment before voters.

Many of the ideas have stalled before, often in Senate committees. The report argues that the new salaries change the calculus, and that the State Ethics Commission already endorses several of the reforms. The group frames the package as bringing New Mexico in line with what most states already require.

Think New Mexico, a nonpartisan think tank founded in 1999, says it accepts no government funding. The report notes that it was researched and written without artificial intelligence.

item.title: Commentary: Otero County's lawmakers, their ethics votes, and the guardrails New Mexico still needs.
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — Before New Mexico voters approved paying legislators a salary, the Legislature took recorded votes on two lobbyist-transparency bills and on the pay amendment itself. Every Otero County legislator voted no on every one of those measures that came before them.

The votes matter as lawmakers prepare for a January session in which Think New Mexico is pressing a package of ethics reforms: recusal on conflicts of interest, a two-year lobbying ban for ex-legislators, fuller lobbyist disclosure and limits on dark money. (Read our story on those proposals.)

Otero County is represented by Rep. John Block (R-Alamogordo, House District 51), Rep. Jonathan Henry (R, House District 54), Sen. Jim Townsend (R, Senate District 34) and Sen. Rex Wilson (R, Senate District 33). Wilson was appointed in January 2026, replacing Sen. Nicholas Paul of Alamogordo, who resigned for health reasons. Rep. Sarah Silva (D-Las Cruces, House District 53), a neighboring southern New Mexico lawmaker, sponsored both lobbying bills.

House Bill 143 (2025) would have required lobbyists to file a report within 48 hours of lobbying on a bill, naming the bill, the client and the position taken. It is the bill-tracking reform Think New Mexico now recommends.

Republicans argued the bill did not go far enough. A House Republican amendment to limit lobbyist spending on lawmakers' meals and drinks was stripped in the Senate. They offered amendments requiring lobbyists to disclose gifts to lawmakers, including food and drink, and requiring grassroots groups to disclose lobbying. Democrats defeated both.

House Bill 164 (2026), a revised version from Silva and Sen. Jeff Steinborn, died on a 32-32 tie on Feb. 14, 2026. Block and Henry again voted no. The vote did not split on party lines: several Democrats, including Reps. Patricia Lundstrom and Linda Serrato, voted no, and Republican Rep. Nicole Chavez voted yes.

The bill died by the narrowest possible margin. A single no vote switched to yes, including from either Otero County House member, would have broken the tie.

House Joint Resolution 5 (2026) put Constitutional Amendment 4 on the ballot, setting legislator pay at the state median household income starting in 2029. It carried no minimum duties, outside-income limits or new ethics rules.

Republicans did try to attach guardrails. In the House, Henry offered an amendment barring per diem on top of a salary for work close to home; Democrats voted it down. In the Senate, Democrats rejected Republican amendments for 16-year term limits and for ending per diem for meetings within 50 miles of a legislator's home.

A competing approach from Republican Sens. Craig Brandt and Pat Boone, Senate Joint Resolution 2, would have had an independent citizens commission set legislative pay, paired with term limits. It did not reach the ballot. That is the model Town News's editorial board urged before the election.

The local delegation's no votes on HJR 5 line up with Town News's objection to pay without guardrails. But their no votes on the lobbying bills cut the other way: those bills were among the few transparency measures to reach a floor vote.

Voters approved a salary. They did not approve a blank check. Three guardrails proposed in the 2025 and 2026 sessions deserve a second chance now that lawmakers will be paid.

Legislators collect $247 a day in per diem during sessions and interim meetings, on top of mileage and a pension. Starting in 2029 they will also draw about $67,800 a year. In a 60-day session year, salary plus session per diem alone reaches $82,620, according to Town News's October analysis.

Per diem exists to cover the cost of being away from home. Paying it to a lawmaker who sleeps in their own bed after a meeting across town is extra pay, not reimbursement. The legislator pension is also calculated from the per diem rate, so every per diem increase raises retirement pay too.

The fixes are modest. Henry's House amendment would have barred per diem on top of salary for work close to home. Senate Republicans proposed ending per diem for meetings within 50 miles of a legislator's home. SJR 2 would have tied per diem to the federal government's lodging rate for Santa Fe. Democrats rejected the first two; SJR 2 never got a hearing.

Lobbyist spending on New Mexico lawmakers set a record in 2025, passing $1.25 million by October. Current reports rarely say which legislators were treated. One 2026 filing listed $22,710 on flowers for legislators; another listed 31 restaurant meals for "various legislators and staff."

State law caps gifts from lobbyists at $250 per donor per year, but meals and entertainment still flow freely during session. In 2025 the House adopted a Republican amendment to HB 143 that many read as a $50-a-day cap on lobbyist spending per legislator during session. The Senate Rules Committee stripped it out.

The bill's Senate sponsor, Sen. Jeff Steinborn, called the cap a distraction from disclosure but said he would back a full ban on such meals in separate legislation. That opening should be taken. A paid legislator has less reason to accept a free dinner from someone seeking their vote.

Sixteen states limit how long legislators may serve. New Mexico does not. In 2026, Senate Republicans proposed a 16-year cap as an amendment to HJR 5, and Sens. Craig Brandt and Pat Boone proposed a 12-year cap in SJR 2. The amendment was rejected and SJR 2 was postponed indefinitely on its first day.

The case is strongest now. A salary turns a citizen post into a paying job, and limits keep it from becoming a career. Turnover breaks up long-standing relationships between lawmakers and the lobbyists who court them, and it opens seats to newcomers in a district like Henry's, where he ran unopposed this year.

Term limits carry real costs, covered below. A 12- to 16-year cap is long enough to let lawmakers build expertise while still forcing regular renewal.

The per diem, meal-cap and term-limit amendments were decided without a recorded roll call, so no individual votes exist in the Legislature's or LegiScan's records. SJR 2 died before any vote. The Legislature broadcasts floor sessions, and these lawmakers can be asked directly where they stand.

Most of what Think New Mexico now proposes has never reached a floor vote, so there is no recorded position for local lawmakers.

The State Ethics Commission cannot carry this load alone, and its own rules show why.

Real accountability means rules with consequences voters can see:

These ideas have serious opponents, and readers should weigh their arguments.

The 60-day legislative session opens Tuesday, Jan. 19, 2027. Block, Henry and Silva won re-election Nov. 3, Wilson won his seat outright, and Townsend's term runs through 2028. All five will be voting. Gov.-elect Deb Haaland takes office Jan. 1, 2027, and will decide whether any reform that passes becomes law.

Lawmakers voted themselves a path to a paycheck. Now it is your turn to set the terms. Call or email every official below before the session opens. Ask each one, by name, to commit publicly to:

Your Otero County legislators

Neighboring southern New Mexico lawmaker

Legislative leadership, which decides which bills get heard

State party leadership

The incoming governor's office

Not sure who represents you? Use the Legislature's district finder.

Capitol offices are staffed mainly during session; email works year-round. A reform that dies in committee never reaches your legislator's vote, so contact leadership, both parties and the governor's office too. Ask for a yes or no. Write down the answer. Then hold them to it at the ballot box.

Related coverage

Official records, HB 143 (2025)

Official records, HB 164 (2026)

Official records, HJR 5 (2026)

Legislators

Guardrails and enforcement

Make the call. Send the email. Demand term limits, a job description and real accountability before the session opens Jan. 19.

item.title: Alamogordo Christmas Miracle Returns for Fifth Year, Calls for Gifts for Babies and Teens
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — The Alamogordo Christmas Miracle is back for its fifth year, and organizer Daniel Acuña has a simple request for holiday shoppers: don't forget the babies and the teenagers.

Speaking with Anthony Lucero on KALH Radio, Acuña said the annual toy drive and community giveaway will take place Saturday, Dec. 12, from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. at Desert Suds Car Wash, which has partnered with the group to host the event.

"Last year we had 400 families come out," Acuña said, "and we helped out a bunch of kids."

The drive collects toys for children from birth through age 17. Acuña said donations tend to cluster around kids roughly 6 to 11, leaving the youngest and oldest children short.

For teenagers, he suggested electronics, sports gear such as footballs, basketballs and soccer balls, personal-care items like deodorant and body wash, and cosmetics, compact mirrors and nail kits.

Collection boxes are set up around town, including two at the Ford dealership, Albertsons, the Classic Desert Aire Hotel, Drinkwell on New York Avenue, Rope Insurance, the Border Patrol, White Sands Dental, George Gandhi, and Jr's Auto Service. New boxes are expected this week at Desert Paws, Betty Dare RE/MAX and Southwest Sound Healing.

Cash donations are also welcome for those unsure what to buy. Gonzalez Lawn, one of the event's platinum sponsors, recently gave $500 toward toys.

Families do not need to sign up in advance, but children must be present to receive a gift. Along with the toy giveaway, the day will feature a live DJ, a car show by Immaculate Car Club, food trucks, vendors, and raffles. Acuña also credited the Saturday market vendors who regularly support the event and will be on hand with crafts for last-minute shoppers.

To donate, volunteer or get more information, contact Acuña through the Alamogordo Christmas Miracle Facebook page, his personal Facebook page (Daniel Acuña), or by phone at 505-410-1375. He stressed that the area code is 505, not 575.

"If you know any kids that need presents this year, send them our way," Acuña said, "and we'll get them something good."

Watch the full interview on Krazy KALH Radio: https://youtu.be/yknacjPDvBw

item.title: Otero County asks feds to pause Sunspot demolition, certifies 2026 election
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — The Otero County Commission on Tuesday, Nov. 10, formally asked the National Science Foundation and the Lincoln National Forest to hold off on tearing down the historic Sacramento Peak Observatory campus at Sunspot. The county wants an independent assessment of which buildings can be saved before any more come down.

The resolution was the centerpiece of a long meeting. Commissioners also certified the 2026 general election canvass, backed a Union Pacific–Norfolk Southern railroad merger with conditions, and approved a regional economic development pact with Lincoln County. They passed a 17-item consent agenda carrying more than $10 million in state infrastructure money.

Chair Vickie Marquardt and Commissioners Gerald Matherly and Amy Barela were all present. The meeting opened with a Veterans Day proclamation honoring the roughly 40 veterans on the county payroll and World War II tank hero Willie E. Estrada, an Otero County native.

Resolution 11-10-26/115-28 asks the NSF and the Forest Service to defer demolition pending a public reuse evaluation. It also requests records on the campus water system and asks that the county be confirmed as a consulting party in the federal historic preservation review. It passed on a motion by Commissioner Matherly.

County Attorney R.B. Nichols said the NSF plans to demolish the campus in phases. A contract has already been awarded to take down the Richard B. Dunn Solar Telescope, where leaking mercury was found earlier this year. A contract for the remaining structures could be awarded anytime between now and March, he said.

Those later phases would take in housing, a dormitory, a community center and a visitor center that drew 12,000 to 15,000 people a year. They would also take in the community water and wastewater system that serves the neighboring Apache Point Observatory and the county's own Sunspot fire station.

Nichols pointed to the NSF's 2019 record of decision, which says buildings or utilities are to be transferred rather than demolished if the Forest Service or another entity identifies a need for them. A 2018 programmatic agreement contemplates the same outcome. "As far as I can tell, that evaluation has not been done," he said.

"Remediation is going to be required, whether the buildings are demolished or preserved," Nichols said. The question, he argued, is whether a building needs "$10,000" of work or is "a $10 million project to save a $500,000 building. We don't know because that detailed assessment has not occurred."

He acknowledged the county is "late to the game." It was not asked to the table, and the issue drew little attention until the mercury leak. But he said New Mexico State University has signaled it would continue research and run the visitor center if an operator can be found for the buildings. NMSU has also obtained quotes for two economic studies on astrotourism potential.

The county has sent the NSF two letters. Nichols said the agency acknowledged them Monday, referred them to its Freedom of Information Act office and classified the county as a "commercial requester." He has written back asking the agency to correct that and to answer the county's request for a pause.

Nichols also raised a federal notice requirement. He said the appropriations act Congress passed in January requires the NSF to notify House and Senate appropriators 30 days before divesting any facility worth more than $2.5 million. The NSF moved ahead with demolition a month after that law took effect and has since obligated at least $13.7 million, he said. He asked the county's congressional delegation to find out whether that notice was given.

Earlier in the meeting, acting Lincoln National Forest Supervisor Cecilia Clavette said the Forest Service shares the goal of preserving Sunspot's history but not its buildings. "We do not believe preserving that history requires preserving the unsafe or deteriorating buildings," she said.

She described an 80-year-old site with asbestos, lead paint and failing utilities, including asbestos water piping underground. Returning the buildings to public use "would require extensive remediation and substantial reinvestment," she said. The current plan grew out of a process that began in 2016 with environmental analysis, historic review and public comment.

Clavette said the agency wants to work with the county on the site's future after cleanup, including a dark-sky recreation area, and on the best path forward for the fire station. Nichols said the Forest Service's vision includes a campground and new visitor center, with most existing buildings removed. Agency officials told him rehabilitation is cost-prohibitive and not in their budget.

Matherly questioned whether demolition is really cheaper. Abatement of asbestos and lead must be paid for either way, he noted, so sealing up some buildings might cost less than tearing them down and hauling debris off the mountain. His top concern, he said, is keeping the water system that is "essential for the mountain community safety."

He also challenged the plan for the Dunn telescope, whose structure extends about 220 feet underground. He said he understood it would be cut down below grade and covered with dirt. That falls short of the full reclamation the Forest Service demands of others, he said, citing the county's old Tully motocross track. "I just want everybody to play by the same rules."

Marquardt said the issue "is just coming to a head now" after years in the works, accelerated by the mercury cleanup. After the vote she told supporters, "We're gonna keep fighting."

Dave Dooling, president of the Sunspot Community Center and the observatory's education officer from 2002 to 2012, said the Dunn's mercury has been removed. It is being held on site in a secure container while the NSF negotiates with the Department of Energy to store it, he said.

His understanding is that the telescope's pieces will be cut away and dropped into the 220-foot pit below, which will then be capped. "There's no contact with an aquifer," he said. He described the $13.7 million as covering assessment, mercury removal and the Dunn's demolition. Later phases could run $15 million to $25 million based on an old NSF estimate adjusted for inflation, he said.

Dooling named three buildings as most worth saving: the visitor center, the Evans Solar Facility and the Hilltop Dome. He said the latter two mainly suffer from peeling paint and could be "mothballed" — an option the NSF itself once considered — until grant money is found. Lead paint and asbestos must be removed before any bulldozing anyway, he noted, "otherwise you turn that stuff into dust" and spread it through the woods.

He said improvements could come in stages and that the community center "could start with dry camping tomorrow if the NSF will let us do it." Sunspot rates a 2 on the 9-point Bortle dark-sky scale, he said: "just about as good as it gets."

Asked whether the county could seek a cease-and-desist order, Dooling said lawyers have told supporters it is hard to direct the federal government on its own property. A cultural heritage lawyer, Ricardo St. Hilaire of New Hampshire, has filed records requests on their behalf, he said. He expects work on the Dunn to start around January, with its contract running through March 23.

Heidi Sanchez, who worked at Sunspot for eight years, spoke remotely after technical trouble. "I'm not saying every building must be saved," she said. "But age alone should not be the justification for demolition. In fact, age is often what makes a place worthy of preservation." She urged a coalition of partners rather than reliance on any single agency. "Once these structures come down, there is no second chance."

Claudia Powell, who spent 10 years with Alamogordo MainStreet, said the architect behind some of Sunspot's 1950s buildings also designed buildings at Los Alamos and the State Capitol Roundhouse. Apart from the science, she said, "this is a really valuable piece of property that we should work really hard to save."

Commissioners certified the canvass of the 2026 general election after a report from County Clerk Selena May. She said 18,158 ballots were cast, for 42% turnout. Same-day registration added 184 voters during early voting and 329 on Election Day.

All polling locations balanced, May said. One provisional ballot was accepted, and 189 ballots were hand-tallied: 80 regular and 109 from military and overseas voters. Ten absentee ballots were rejected — four for missing signatures or Social Security digits, and six with no outer envelope or with the identifying sticker removed.

The one significant problem came in Chaparral, where a polling site ran low on ballot paper. Replacement stock borrowed from Doña Ana County turned out to be 17-inch paper, not Otero's 14-inch, and 26 voters waited about 15 minutes for the right stock. "Longest 15 minutes of my life," May said. Everyone in line got to vote.

May said this was the last election in Room 101 of the county administration building. On Sheriff David Black's advice, the clerk's office will no longer hold early voting there because the building must stay open to the public for long stretches. Officials cited people entering to use the restrooms, including at least one homeless person this cycle. The county is seeking a new early voting site and has until next June to set polling locations.

The consent agenda passed in a single vote. Major items included:

The board also endorsed New Mexico Counties' 2027 legislative priorities, November budget adjustments, an FY2027 sick leave buyback and quarterly financial reports. It awarded the state lobbyist contract to DeVore Aragon.

The commission closed with an executive session to discuss litigation and the purchase, acquisition or disposal of real property.

item.title: Diaz Runs to Fourth as Mescalero Apache, Cloudcroft Close Season at State
item.description:
ALBUQUERQUE — Mescalero Apache standout Azellia Diaz raced to a fourth-place finish and led her team to an eighth-place team showing at Saturday's NMAA Class 2A State Cross Country Championships at Albuquerque Academy, capping a strong season for both Mescalero Apache and Cloudcroft.

In the team standings, the Mescalero Apache girls placed 8th and the Cloudcroft girls 12th. On the boys' side, Cloudcroft finished 10th, one spot ahead of Mescalero Apache in 11th.

Diaz was the class of the local field, covering the course in 20:35.02 to claim fourth overall against the state's best 2A runners. Malair Maldonado gave Mescalero a second strong scorer, finishing 33rd in 22:55.15, and Rhiannon Blazer added a 51st-place run in 23:42.43.

Stephie Prins (74th, 26:03.97) and Verbena Comanche (75th, 26:22.78) crossed the line just seconds apart to round out the scoring five, followed by Ellie Gallerito (82nd, 27:30.78) and Lariah Comanche (86th, 28:16.02).

Gena Davis paced the Cloudcroft girls, finishing 43rd in 23:25.99. Adelyn Tompkins was next in 72nd (25:55.88), followed by Bella Johnson in 81st (27:17.64), Brisa Johnson in 88th (29:20.34) and Alyssa Singer in 90th (29:57.55).

Fin Abel led Cloudcroft and was the top local finisher in the boys' race, placing 35th in 18:19.46. Triston Tompkins (59th, 19:37.44) and Forrest Odom (67th, 20:00.11) followed, with Tyler Meszler (78th, 20:48.48) and Ryder Kempf (80th, 20:51.95) separated by just three and a half seconds at the back of the scoring five. Rafael Pulido (90th, 23:28.56) and Raine Langford (91st, 24:08.26) completed the Cloudcroft lineup.

Shywin Chaffins led Mescalero Apache with a 41st-place finish in 18:36.73. Damien Valez came in 66th (19:54.91) and Travien Comanche 72nd (20:28.60), followed by Kanin Fernando in 89th (22:43.88), Ricardo Yuzos in 92nd (24:17.57) and Eustine Chino in 93rd (24:46.42).

With all four squads qualifying for the state meet and Diaz earning a top-five finish, Saturday's championships were a fitting end to a fantastic season for the Mescalero Apache and Cloudcroft cross country programs. Congratulations to all the runners and coaches.

Full results are available on MileSplit New Mexico.

item.title: The Doctor Is In: Could the City Have Settled Its Open Meetings Fight for Less?
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — Former City Manager Dr. Stephanie Hernandez says the Alamogordo City Commission could have resolved its Open Meetings Act dispute months ago, without running up outside legal bills. She made the case on this week's "The Doctor Is In" segment with host Anthony Lucero on KALH Radio.

The segment centers on the citizen lawsuit over the hiring of City Manager Robert Stockwell. Chris Edwards and Concerned Citizens of Alamogordo filed the petition in the Twelfth Judicial District Court on June 2, 2026, after giving the City written notice of the alleged violations on May 5 (background). A judge has since refused to dismiss the case, and it is headed for a hearing on the merits (court ruling).

"Could this have been resolved months ago without spending taxpayer dollars on outside legal representation?" Hernandez asked.

Hernandez said that while she was still city manager, she recommended the Commission acknowledge a potential violation, disclose it voluntarily and take corrective action.

State law gives public bodies room to do that. Before a citizen can sue, the public body gets written notice and 15 days to act on the claim, and it can reconsider a challenged action at a properly noticed public meeting. Violations are also a misdemeanor, punishable by a fine of up to $500 per offense against an individual who is convicted.

"To me, voluntarily identifying and correcting a potential violation seemed far less costly than prolonged litigation," she said. She added that a voluntary fix could still be an option today, though it would not guarantee the lawsuit is dismissed.

Hernandez also addressed concerns raised at the time that she had a conflict of interest, since the dispute involved hiring her successor. Her recommendation, she said, was about protecting the City and taxpayers, not about who should hold the job.

Hernandez pointed to Commissioner Baxter Pattillo's description of doing the legwork on Stockwell's proposed contract and circulating documents to the Commission.

That, she said, raises the possibility of a rolling quorum: commissioners discussing public business through a series of private communications that together involve a quorum. She was careful to note that circulating documents is not necessarily a violation on its own, but said it raises questions worth examining.

Hernandez acknowledged the law is complicated. She said she has worked with it for seven years and still doesn't consider herself an expert. Still, she noted, the Commission received Open Meetings Act training in March and has had earlier training opportunities.

Hernandez pushed back on the idea that the City can simply recover its legal bills from the citizen if it prevails.

Under the Open Meetings Act, a winning public body is awarded court costs. It recovers attorney fees only if the court also finds the plaintiff sued without sufficient information and belief that good grounds supported the case (NMSA 10-15-3).

"A citizen seeking government transparency doesn't automatically become responsible for the City's attorney fees simply because they lose a lawsuit," she said. The longer the case runs, she added, the higher the bills climb.

"Government officials make mistakes. What matters is how they respond," Hernandez said. "Shouldn't protecting taxpayer dollars be just as important as winning a lawsuit?"

Hear the full conversation with Dr. Stephanie Hernandez and Anthony Lucero on "The Doctor Is In": Open Meetings Act — The Doctor Is In (YouTube). More programming at KALHRadio.org.

Disclosure: Chris Edwards, general manager of KALH Radio and Alamogordo Town News, is the petitioner in the lawsuit discussed here. The case continues with an expected motion ruling within a week and a court conference to discuss next steps.

item.title: 2nd Life Media Alamogordo Town News Alamogordo Honors Its Veterans on Veterans Day 2026
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — At 11 a.m. today, Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026, Alamogordo pauses to honor the men and women who have worn the uniform of the United States. In a city whose story has been tied to Holloman Air Force Base since 1942, Veterans Day is not an abstraction. It is the neighbor down the street, the retiree at the VFW, and the Airman who just came home from deployment.

The 108th anniversary of the World War I armistice falls midweek this year, so the community began its tribute early. Since Saturday, residents have lined 10th Street, filled the civic center and gathered at the airport to say thank you.

The observances opened Saturday, Nov. 7, with the annual Veterans Day Parade down 10th Street from Cuba Avenue to Maryland Avenue. The free parade was organized by Air Force Sergeants Association Chapter 1257 at Holloman (Town News).

Airmen of the 49th Wing marched alongside cadets of the Alamogordo High School Air Force Junior ROTC, and the Tiger marching band played the route (DVIDS). The Patriot Guard Riders staged that morning at Mountain View Church on Cuba Avenue to ride in the procession (Patriot Guard Riders).

The same day, the Alamogordo-White Sands Regional Airport held a free Open House and Veterans Appreciation Day with aircraft displays, food trucks and STEM activities. The city's Sounds of Freedom celebration filled Alameda Park (City of Alamogordo). On Tuesday night, AFSA Chapter 1257 hosted its 13th annual Veterans Appreciation Dinner at the Sgt. Willie Estrada Memorial Civic Center, free to local veterans and a guest.

Few New Mexico communities are as bound to the armed forces as Alamogordo. This past May, the city and Holloman received the 2025 Altus Community Support Award, their second win in three years (Holloman AFB). The honor recognizes the city's backing of the base and its families.

That bond keeps growing. In June the 49th Wing welcomed Col. Michael S. Mullin as commander, back for a second tour, as the wing moved to Air Combat Command (Town News). In July six 49th Wing Airmen, including two Security Forces leaders awarded the Bronze Star, were recognized for combat service in the Middle East (Air University). They are today's veterans in the making.

The city's older generations are honored, too. In April, Vietnam-era veterans Chris Hall and Lucio Vazquez came home from a Rio Grande Honor Flight trip to Washington, D.C., to a hero's welcome at Patron's Hall (Town News). Over Memorial Day weekend, more than 70 volunteers joined VFW Post 7686 at dawn to place flags on veterans' graves at Monte Vista Cemetery (Town News).

Groups like the U.S. Veterans MC Trinity Chapter, chartered here in 2018 on a mission of veterans helping veterans, carry that service forward all year (Town News).

The parade may be over, but there are simple ways to honor veterans today and beyond:

Veterans seeking benefits help can contact the New Mexico Department of Veterans' Services. Any veteran in crisis, or anyone worried about one, can call or text 988 and press 1 for the Veterans Crisis Line, available around the clock.

From the F-16s over the Tularosa Basin to the flags at Monte Vista Cemetery, Alamogordo lives alongside its service members every day. Today the city simply says it out loud.

To every veteran, active-duty member and military family in Alamogordo, Holloman, Tularosa and beyond: thank you for your service.

Note article by Chris Edwards, a journalist for 2nd Life Media affiliated sites. Mr Edwards is a strong advocate and supporter of the mission of the Honor Flights, the local VFW’s upgrades and its impact of support as a safe and diverse gathering place for our veterans, and supporting the mission of team Holloman and all of our area veterans.

item.title: Solar developer pitches three sites near Tularosa as neighbors press on flooding
item.description:
TULAROSA — A community solar developer told the Tularosa Planning and Zoning Commission on Tuesday that it hopes to build as many as three solar gardens in and around the village. Neighbors of one proposed site said they don't oppose solar power, but they urged officials to make sure the project doesn't worsen flooding that already damages their property.

SunShare Community Solar has filed special use permit applications for all three sites. The company says it built its first project in Colorado Springs in 2011. It now reports more than 220 megawatts developed, about 19,000 subscribers and operations in nine states.

"We're really excited to talk to you guys about three community solar gardens that we are proposing within the village of Tularosa," said Mike, an associate developer with the company. He presented with Keenan, SunShare's director of development for New Mexico.

Under New Mexico's Community Solar Act, passed in 2021, residents and small businesses can subscribe to a solar garden and receive credits on their PNM bills. SunShare said standard subscribers save 10%.

State rules require at least 30% of each project's output to go to low-income subscribers, at a discount of at least 20%. SunShare said its projects typically reserve 50% for low-income households and give them a 30% discount. New Mexico lets residents self-attest to low-income status.

Each project would be about 5 megawatts, enough for roughly 400 to 500 subscribers, according to the company. Signing up and opting out are free. The power would flow to PNM's Tularosa substation and be used locally.

Two sites sit off Moon Valley Road. The first, which SunShare calls the Cumbre project, lies next to an existing solar array built by a different company. A smaller parcel lies to its northeast. The third site is on the north side of town off Twelfth Street, with the railroad along its west edge.

SunShare said it bought one property and is leasing the other two. Leases run 20 years with optional five-year extensions, and each site needs about 30 acres. State rules require projects to be within a mile of a three-phase power line, which representatives said explains why the sites are close to homes.

The company described sites with an 8-foot, wildlife-friendly security fence, no lighting and no batteries. It said inverters run about 58 decibels and can't be heard beyond roughly 150 feet. SunShare said it would replant native vegetation, use no chemical herbicides and post a bond to cover eventual decommissioning.

Ann Farmer, who lives on Highway 54/70 just south of the proposed Moon Valley sites, told commissioners she has no complaint about solar panels themselves.

"I have no problem with the solar field itself because I've already got one across from me," Farmer said. "They're good neighbors. They're quiet. They don't block my view."

Her concern is drainage. Farmer said flooding from a nearby arroyo has gotten worse every year since a pellet plant built a bridge over it. The last storm washed out her driveway and reached the highway, partly closing the road into town, she said. Sediment has now built up higher than her land, and her family keeps having to raise the berm that protects her house.

"The good news is we don't have that much rain, but when it comes, it just about wipes me out," she said. She said a culvert near her neighbor's driveway stays clogged. When the state tried to clean it out, it left deep ruts, she said, and she got no reply after emailing photos to the highway department.

Rick Robbins, a 75-year-old retired military veteran who has lived on Moon Valley Road for 30 years, raised the same flooding concern. "It doesn't even have to rain here in Tularosa," he said. "If it rains on the mountain over there, it funnels down and comes across Moon Valley Road."

Robbins asked who would maintain the private road that construction crews would use. He also asked whether the panels would raise nearby temperatures, citing research he found that put the increase as high as 6 degrees. He also asked about snakes and wildlife, future expansion and property values.

SunShare representatives said they had already spoken with the landowner about the arroyo. They offered to add regular ditch cleanouts to the site's maintenance contract.

"There has never been, I guess, an actual agreement in place for someone to actually do that," one representative said. "I think this is an opportunity for us to actually address it." The company also noted that a stormwater management plan is required before it can get a building permit.

On roads, SunShare said it would sign a road use agreement, post a bond if the village requires one and repair any damage. On heat, representatives said studies of the "heat island effect" show solar arrays are not a significant concern. They said panels on single-axis trackers move through the day and trap far less heat than a parking lot.

The company said program rules allow only one project per parcel, which limits expansion. On property values, a representative said studies have found effects in both directions. SunShare said glare studies for all three sites found no impacts, and early environmental and cultural reviews came back favorable.

The commission took no vote Tuesday. For special use permits, the commission doesn't approve or deny. It sends findings of fact and conditional recommendations to the Village Council, which makes the decision. Commissioners said SunShare would get a copy of their findings.

Any approval would also depend on a state contest. The projects are competing in Phase 2 of the community solar program, a competitive request for proposals run by the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission. SunShare expects bidding to open in January or February. Awards are expected around June 2027.

"Maybe we are able to get one project or two projects, maybe all three, or maybe none," Keenan said. SunShare confirmed it cannot build without a state award. If it wins, construction would likely start in early 2028 and take about three months.

Commissioners raised possible conditions, including a list of native plants, a decommissioning bond that rises each year with inflation, and an access easement for the village in case it annexes the areas, which are now in its extraterritorial jurisdiction. SunShare said it was open to each.

Opportunity zone. The commission heard that Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham has nominated three Otero County census tracts for federal opportunity zone designation, one of them in Tularosa. The others cover Alamogordo's downtown and the corridor along the Charlie Lee Memorial Relief Route. The designation would give investors federal tax breaks for putting money into those areas from 2027 through 2036. Commissioners said federal approval is usually routine. They stressed that the village needs updated ordinances in place before investors arrive: vacant building registration, then development impact fees, then a historic preservation plan.

State permit dispute. The commission approved the permit for a completed re-roof at 710 First Street. The state Construction Industries Division had issued its own permit without going through the village. Village staff said they have written to all three CID offices and are following up by phone. The homeowner paid the village fee after the work was done.

Code enforcement. Commissioners can now issue a first-notice form for planning and zoning violations, created by the village's code enforcement officer, who will handle follow-up. Residents with complaints can call the police non-emergency line. The village's ordinances can be searched on its website.

New member. The commission welcomed new member Efren Gonzalez.

The meeting adjourned at 6:50 p.m.

item.title: Tigers Get Hometown Send-Off Before 5A Quarterfinal at Los Lunas
item.description:
Alamogordo N.M. - The Alamogordo Tigers are hitting the road for the biggest game of their season, and the town is being asked to give them a proper goodbye.

Alamogordo High School will hold a Tiger Football Playoff Send-Off at 2 p.m. Friday, Nov. 13, as the team departs for Saturday's Class 5A state quarterfinal against Los Lunas. Organizers are calling on students, families, alumni, local businesses and the wider community to turn out in black and gold.

Fans who can't make it to the school are encouraged to find a spot anywhere along the route to cheer the bus as it passes.

It's a Tigers-vs.-Tigers matchup. Fifth-seeded Alamogordo (7-4) earned the trip with a dominant 54-0 first-round shutout of district rival Chaparral last Friday, its fifth straight win. Over that five-game streak, Alamogordo's defense has given up just 47 points combined — fewer than it allowed in its season opener alone.

The offense was balanced against Chaparral. Junior quarterback Nathaniel Cereceres threw for 141 yards and two touchdowns and ran for 69 yards and another score on just seven carries. Junior receiver Tristan Bowman piled up 111 receiving yards, including a 76-yard catch, and scored both through the air and on the ground. Sophomore running back Qymani Patterson added 110 rushing yards and a touchdown, breaking off a 45-yard run.

Los Lunas (7-3) is in its first season in Class 5A after moving down from 6A and earned the No. 4 seed and a first-round bye under first-year head coach Stephen Johnston. The hosts are rolling too: they closed the regular season with a 50-0 rout of Highland, and quarterback Luke Cieremans threw four touchdown passes in that game. Los Lunas' defense has allowed only 33 points over its last seven games.

First-round results (Nov. 6–7)

Roswell, Piedra Vista, Artesia and Los Lunas had first-round byes as the top four seeds.

Quarterfinals (Nov. 13–14)

What's next: Semifinals are Nov. 20–21, and the Class 5A state championship is Nov. 28 at a finalist's home site. A win Saturday would put Alamogordo in the final four.

Other quarterfinals this weekend include Class 6A's No. 1 Cleveland hosting No. 9 Rio Rancho and No. 2 Volcano Vista hosting No. 7 Carlsbad; Class 4A's No. 1 Bloomfield hosting No. 8 Valencia; and Class 3A's No. 1 St. Michael's hosting No. 8 Pojoaque Valley. Six-man crowns its champion Nov. 14, eight-man on Nov. 21, and Classes 2A through 6A on Nov. 28.

item.title: In Memory of Norman Lane
item.description:
Norman Lane, 93, passed away peacefully on September 6, 2026, in Las Cruces, New Mexico. Born and raised in Cloudcroft, New Mexico, he later made Alamogordo his home for 68 years, eventually moving to Las Cruces, NM for health care.

Norman proudly served in the United States Navy during the Korean War. After his military service, he built a successful career as a businessman and land developer. His ventures included Lane Plumbing Co., inc. in 1962, Lane Good Housekeeping Store, Desert Hills Subdivision and many others. He gave generously of his time to the community through his involvement with the Noon Lions Club, the Masonic Lodge, and the Elks Lodge. He was also a longtime member of Grace United Methodist Church.

Norman is survived by his three children, Gary Lane (Wanda), Cheri Rabon (Randy), Debbie Moore; his seven grandchildren, Kayla Lane, Norman Jaret Lane (Katie), Kelsey Joy Lane, Kristy Alsleben (Matt), Chad Rabon (Paige), Cody Lane Craig (Nikki), Abe Moore (Juliett), Josh Moore (Christine); his 14 great grandchildren.

Family was at the heart of Norman's life. He was preceded in death by Joy, the love of his life. Together, they shared 69 wonderful years of marriage. He was also preceded in death by his parents, Les and Jennie Lane; his brothers, Rex "Buster" Lane, Gene Lane, Dutch Lane; his son-in-law, Doug Moore; his grandson, Eli Moore.

He leaves behind many special friends including his dear friend, Yvonne Brown, as well as countless lives he touched over the years.

Those who knew Norman will remember his strong work ethic, outgoing spirit, and love of life. He never met a stranger and enjoyed connecting with people wherever he went. He loved classic cars, traveling in his RV, watching sports, and spending many years making memories at Elephant Butte lake.

More than anything, Norman's greatest legacy was his family. He will be deeply missed and lovingly remembered by his children, grandchildren, great grandchildren, extended family, and many friends. He often told anyone who would listen how blessed he was and how grateful he felt to have lived 93 full and meaningful years.

A Celebration of Life will be held for Norman from 1:00 pm to 3:00 pm on Monday, November 23, 2026, at the Elks Lodge located at 2290 Hamilton Road in Alamogordo.

item.title: Alamogordo commission to weigh mayor's agenda role, closed-door complaint against city manager
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — A  dispute in interpretation of Charter rules between Mayor Sharon McDonald and City Manager Robert Stockwell will play out on two fronts Tuesday, when the Alamogordo City Commission is set to decide how much control the mayor should have over meeting agendas and, behind closed doors, to consider a complaint involving Stockwell himself.

The regular meeting begins at 6:30 p.m. Nov. 17 in the Donald E. Carroll City Commission Chambers at City Hall, 1376 E. Ninth St.

Under an item titled "the Mayor's Role in the City Commission Agenda Process," Stockwell asks commissioners to clarify Rule 5(a) of Resolution 2018-08, which says only that the city clerk "shall consult with the City Manager and the Mayor" when preparing agendas.

According to Stockwell's written report in the agenda packet, McDonald recently emailed him and City Clerk Rachel Hughs saying she would take a more active role in building and finalizing agendas. She asked to receive a preliminary draft of each agenda with enough time to review it and meet with both officials before publication, and to be consulted on any later removal or significant change to agenda items. McDonald wrote that as presiding officer she has "a responsibility to be informed and adequately prepared," according to the report.

Stockwell argues the request adds steps that could delay getting the full packet to commissioners. Agenda items are due at noon the Tuesday before a meeting, he wrote, and building in time for the mayor's review would push that deadline back to the previous Friday. He noted that past mayors have occasionally sat in on agenda review meetings but were never given approval authority, and that the agenda is not formally adopted until the full commission votes on it at the start of each meeting.

Stockwell said he directed the clerk to follow the mayor's process for Tuesday's agenda, and his report lays out how that went: the first draft went to McDonald at 10:18 a.m. on a Tuesday, revisions followed at 3:04 p.m., and a reminder that staff were awaiting her approval went out at 4:45 p.m. McDonald gave her approval at 4:54 a.m. the next day, the report says. Stockwell added that an error was later found in identifying which department director the mayor wanted investigated, requiring yet another review before the agenda could be finalized.

"If the City Commission feels the request of the Mayor to enlarge her role in the agenda process is appropriate, then Rule 5(a) should be amended to clarify the process," Stockwell wrote.

Stockwell's report quotes from McDonald's email but does not include it. The full text of the email, addressed to Stockwell and City Clerk Rachel Hughs, reads:

City Manager Stockwell and City Clerk Hughs,

I am requesting that, effective immediately, I be included in the review of all City Commission agendas before they are finalized and published.

Under Resolution No. 2018-08, Rule 5(a), the City Clerk is required to consult with both the City Manager and the Mayor in preparing the agenda. Additionally, Rule 5(c) establishes that any Commission member may direct that matters within the Commission's jurisdiction be placed on the agenda.

As Mayor and presiding officer of the City Commission meetings I have a responsibility to be informed and adequately prepared for the business coming before the governing body. Meaningful participation in the agenda preparation process allows me to fulfill that responsibility, identify potential concerns, and ensure that matters requiring Commission consideration are appropriately presented.

While I recognize your respective administrative responsibilities, the agenda serves the governing body, and my involvement should occur before it is finalized.

Moving forward, I would like to receive a preliminary draft of each agenda with sufficient time to review it and meet with both of you before publication. I also expect to be consulted regarding any proposed removal or significant modification of agenda items following our review meeting.

This is not about interfering with administrative responsibilities. It is about ensuring that the Mayor's responsibilities and the procedures established by the City Commission are respected.

Please confirm that this review process will be incorporated into the preparation of future Commission agendas.

Thank you,

Mayor Sharon McDonald, City of Alamogordo

The email asks for review before publication and consultation on later changes. It does not claim authority to approve or veto agenda items. Stockwell's report contrasts the request with past mayors, who he says did their jobs "without asserting a role of approving drafts and the final submission" of the agenda.

Alamogordo has a commission-manager form of government: an elected commission sets policy and hires a manager to run the city day to day.

State law. Under NMSA 1978 Section 3-14-10, the mayor "shall preside at all meetings of the commission and perform other duties, consistent with his/her office, as imposed by the commission," and holds all the powers of a commissioner, including a vote on every question. Section 3-14-12 vests the city's governing powers in the commission as a body, and Sections 3-14-13 and 3-14-14 give daily administration to the manager. The law gives the mayor no administrative authority of her own, but leaves the commission free to assign her additional duties.

The city charter. Article VIII, Section 2 of the Alamogordo City Charter makes the mayor the presiding officer of commission meetings and the representative and voice of the city. 

The commission's own rules. Resolution 2018-08 sets the commission's meeting procedures. Rule 5(a) states that "the City Clerk shall consult with the City Manager and the Mayor" in preparing the agenda. The consultation is required, but the rule does not say when it must happen, what form it takes, or whether the mayor may approve, change or hold back items.

Past practice. Stockwell's report acknowledges that mayors have "on occasion" attended agenda review meetings with the manager and clerk, though he says those meetings never gave a mayor approval authority. McDonald has said pre-publication agenda meetings were routine under her three predecessors — Susie Galea, Richard Boss and Susan Payne — and that she is asking to restore that practice, not create a new one.

Former Mayor Susan Payne confirms McDonald’s assessment and disputes Stockwell’s assertion as an attempt to undermine over two decades of precedent. 

What commissioners must decide. The dispute comes down to what "consult" means. Read narrowly, as Stockwell reads it, the requirement is met by the existing manager-clerk review, with the agenda finalized when the full commission votes on it at the start of each meeting. Read broadly, it calls for the mayor's input while the agenda is still being drafted. Because state law lets the commission define the mayor's additional duties, commissioners can settle the question by leaving Rule 5(a) as written or by amending it to spell out the process — the option Stockwell's report raises.

Public comment is encouraged as the mayor is the only at large publicly elected official on the commission to represent the public at large.

Later in the meeting, the commission is scheduled to recess into executive session to discuss "the consideration and possible investigation of a complaint concerning the City Manager and the Community Development Director," an item placed on the agenda by McDonald. Shelley Dowhanik-Baron is the city's community development director.

The agenda lists a possible follow-up vote in open session to authorize an independent investigation of the complaint. The packet does not say who filed the complaint or what it alleges, and no supporting documents were included.

The city has no city attorney; the position is listed as vacant on the agenda. Resolutions in the packet are signed "approved as to form" by Stockwell.

Personnel issues in the Community Development Department have surfaced at recent meetings. During public comment on Oct. 27, former employee Justen Boyle told commissioners he believed his firing was retaliation for raising ADA-compliance and ordinance concerns with human resources, and that his grievance hearing was canceled with less than 24 hours' notice, according to draft minutes. At the same meeting, commissioners voted 7-0 after a closed session to have HR Director Michelle Osborne hire an independent reviewer for a separate personnel matter involving the city's senior project manager, with a deadline of Nov. 17. The agenda does not indicate whether either matter is connected to the new complaint.

Commissioners will also meet privately to discuss real property — specifically the sale of the Fairgrounds parking lot — with a possible vote afterward to authorize the sale. The packet does not name a buyer or a price.

On the consent agenda, Resolution 2026-38 would impose a six-month moratorium on new off-premise billboards, including new electronic billboards and conversions of existing billboards to electronic displays.

It would be the city's seventh such moratorium since 2018. The most recent one expired June 2, 2026. The resolution says billboards "can significantly detract" from the city's goals for aesthetics and image, and that the pause is meant to hold while the city updates its code of ordinances, including its sign rules. It covers elevated off-premise signs at least 4 feet off the ground with a face of 100 square feet or more.

Residents who want to speak during public comment must sign up with the city clerk; the standard time limit is three minutes. The full agenda packet is posted on the city's website. People needing disability accommodations should contact the City Clerk's Office at 575-439-4100 at least 48 hours in advance.

Sources: IPRA and City of Alamogordo Regular Meeting Agenda Book, Nov. 17, 2026, including agenda reports and draft minutes of the Oct. 27 and Nov. 3, 2026, meetings; Alamogordo City Charter; Resolution 2018-08; NMSA 1978, Sections 3-14-10 through 3-14-14.

item.title: Alamogordo Police Weekly Log: Shots-Fired Arrest, Four DWIs and a Busy Week for Animal Control, November 2–8, 2026

People named in police reports are presumed innocent until proven guilty in a court of law.
